title: Gideon and the Radiators
premise: After her mother's funeral, Tamsin Brightwater returns to the decaying family house to catalog its contents before sale, discovering a notebook of songs her mother wrote but never recorded or performed. When a local radio station plays one of them—note for note—Tamsin realizes someone else has been inside her mother's silence, and the inheritance she assumed was hers alone is shared with a stranger. Following the song's trail, she uncovers her mother's hidden life: a brief, formative love, an abandoned band, and a final untranslated sentence written in a language Tamsin doesn't speak. In the novel's climax, Tamsin performs the songs at the house's last open evening, claiming the inheritance by voice rather than blood; the resolution finds her translating the final sentence—'I stayed so you could go'—and leaving the house empty on her own terms.
about_author: Bram Underhill is the pen name of a former estate auctioneer who spent a decade cataloguing the belongings of the recently bereaved. They write literary fiction about the objects and silences families leave behind, and live in a converted chapel on the Yorkshire coast.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Inventory
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Three weeks after the funeral, Tamsin moves through her mother's house room by room with a legal pad, cataloguing for the estate sale. She sleeps in the guest room, unable to enter the master bedroom. The emotional beat is numb displacement: she is an heir who feels like a lodger, and the house feels like it's already been sold.

chapters.title: Room With the Door Shut
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. The solicitor sets a six-week deadline for the sale. Tamsin finally opens her mother's bedroom and finds a locked cedar chest beneath the window. Inside: sheet music, dozens of songs in her mother's handwriting, none titled, none dated. The beat is the first crack in grief—curiosity arriving uninvited, like an intruder.

chapters.title: Songs Nobody Sang
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. She reads the songs aloud in the empty kitchen, half-singing, and realizes they are good—strange, private, complete. Her memory of her mother as a silent, practical woman begins to warp. The beat is dissonance: the woman in the songs and the woman who raised her refuse to be the same person.

chapters.title: Static, Then a Voice
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Driving to town for packing supplies, a late-night community radio program plays a song Tamsin recognizes from the chest—note for note, lyric for lyric. The host credits 'a local writer, deceased last month, by family arrangement.' Tamsin pulls over, shaking. The beat is vertigo: her mother's silence has been broadcast, and someone arranged it.

chapters.title: The Man Who Answered
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. She tracks the station to its host, Deshawn Okafor, a retired music teacher who received the tapes anonymously with funeral details attached. He knows only that the sender's handwriting matched a name: R. Voss. Tamsin has never heard the name. The beat is the first alliance—grief finding a witness outside the family.

chapters.title: R. Voss
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. In the town library's microfilm, she finds Roderick Voss: a bassist in a band her mother played with for one year, 1974, before vanishing from every record. A group photo shows her mother laughing, guitar in hand, unrecognizable. The beat is betrayal sharpening into hunger—who was she, and why did she stop?

chapters.title: What the Aunts Knew
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. She confronts her aunt Marion, who admits the family knew: the music was 'the year we don't discuss,' ended when her mother chose respectability and a marriage Tamsin's father. Marion begs her to let the dead stay dead. The beat is generational pressure—the inheritance of silence being actively enforced.

chapters.title: The Untranslated Page
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. At the back of the notebook, one song's lyrics are written in a language Tamsin can't identify, in a different, older hand. Below it, her mother wrote a single English line: 'Translate this before you leave.' The beat is dread turning to summons: her mother anticipated her here, decades ago.

chapters.title: Buyer's Agent at the Door
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. The house sale accelerates; a developer's agent tours the property, measuring rooms, praising the light. Tamsin stalls the paperwork, lying about probate delays. Her brother Callum arrives, furious, insisting she's sabotaging their inheritance. The beat is external pressure closing in—time and money against memory.

chapters.title: Callum's Version
chapters.summary: POV Callum. The novel's one shift: Callum remembers a different mother—warm to him, cold to Tamsin—and believes the songs are Tamsin's way of monopolizing grief. His anger masks his own unreadiness to lose the house. The beat is sibling fracture: two children inheriting two different women.

chapters.title: The Language of the Page
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. A university linguist identifies the script as an obscure dialect from her grandmother's home village—her mother's mother tongue, never spoken at home. The untranslated song is a lullaby, and the handwriting is the grandmother's. The beat is deepening inheritance: the silence is three generations old.

chapters.title: Letters to Roderick
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. She locates Voss, now a luthier in a coastal town, and he gives her the surviving tapes and letters: her mother at twenty-two, ferociously talented, planning to leave. The letters end mid-year. Voss says only, 'Ask her why she stayed. I never got an answer.' The beat is a door opening onto a question, not an answer.

chapters.title: The Year We Don't Discuss
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Reassembling the year from tapes, letters, and a bandmate's diary, Tamsin learns her mother was offered a recording contract—and withdrew days after learning she was pregnant with Tamsin, choosing the house, the marriage, the silence. The beat is devastating ambiguity: was it sacrifice, or was it fear?

chapters.title: Probate and Pressure
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Callum forces the sale timeline; the developer's offer is accepted unless Tamsin can match it, which she cannot. Deshawn offers to air the remaining songs as a memorial broadcast, but Tamsin hesitates—it isn't hers to give. The beat is the cost of stewardship: honoring the dead may mean disobeying the living.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's House
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. She travels to her grandmother's village and finds a great-aunt who remembers the lullaby and sings it back to her. Its meaning: a mother's promise to leave so the child could belong elsewhere. Tamsin records it on her phone, hands shaking. The beat is the past answering the present across three generations of women.

chapters.title: What Tamsin Carried
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Returning, she realizes her own life has gone tenant-shaped: a sublet, a paused career, a relationship she never moved into. The songs have been asking her the question her mother never answered aloud—what do you stay for, and what does staying cost? The beat is the mirror turning inward.

chapters.title: The Offer She Refuses
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. The developer offers her a job curating 'heritage features' of the house in their showrooms—her mother's things as marketing. Callum urges her to take it. Tamsin refuses, and their rupture goes nuclear: he accuses her of loving the dead more than the living. The beat is the lowest point—inheritance as weapon.

chapters.title: The Last Open Evening
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Before handover, Tamsin hosts an uninvited farewell in the emptying house: neighbors, Voss, Deshawn with a portable recorder, even a reluctant Callum in the doorway. She performs the songs, ending with the lullaby in the grandmother's tongue, untranslatable and sung anyway. The beat is the climax—claiming inheritance by voice, in the house's final hours.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Deshawn airs the recording; strangers call in with their own unrecorded mothers, their own cedar chests. Callum, listening in his car outside the house, finally comes in and sits with her among the boxes. The beat is thaw: grief shared becomes inheritance rather than theft.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Translated
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. With Voss and the great-aunt's recording, Tamsin completes the translation of the final line: 'I stayed so you could go.' She understands it both ways at once—her mother's sacrifice and her mother's command. The beat is the thematic keystone: silence decoded, and it is both wound and permission.

chapters.title: Closing
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. The sale completes. Tamsin walks the empty rooms one last time, leaves the notebook's duplicate pages in the cedar chest for the house's next life, and takes only the original and her mother's guitar. The beat is release without erasure—she leaves as an owner of her own story, not a tenant of her mother's.

chapters.title: First Song, Second Life
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin, epilogue-like. Months later, in a small rented flat she chose herself, Tamsin records the songs properly with Voss and Deshawn, titling the album with the translated sentence. The last image is her voice in a live room, the silence finally broken and hers to carry forward. The beat is resolution: inheritance completed, identity claimed, memory made audible.
